extracted.intended_audience: researchers (especially early-career) asked to perform journal peer reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers on how to perform rigorous, ethical, and constructive peer review of journal manuscripts (particularly for journals like PeerJ/PLOS ONE). Covers ethical practices, how to read and evaluate sections of a paper, and procedural considerations such as anonymity and post-publication review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself honestly whether this paper falls within the scope of your expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it falls too far outside your discipline and knowledge, decline the review. If you decline, do so promptly (to avoid delaying the process) and recommend several alternate referees to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an effort to return a review within the specified deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider your schedule and the time required (complicated papers take more time — author estimates given: ~8–10 hours for a full review and ~4 hours for a revised version). If you can't commit the time, decline or request an extension before accepting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take it seriously / Rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a rigorous, critical review rather than a cursory 'sign off'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the manuscript critically and thoroughly; the review should help authors improve the manuscript and contribute to the journal's quality. Don't do a slapdash job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not review if you have strong positive/negative feelings about the authors, or any possible conflict of interest (e.g., prior collaboration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, declare the possible conflict before agreeing. Be aware of implicit biases (gender, location, etc.) and make a deliberate effort to review the manuscript in front of you, not the authors or their location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from hierarchical intimidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be intimidated by authors' seniority or reputation; evaluate the work on its merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implicit academic hierarchy should not apply in reviewing — big names are not automatically right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain confidentiality about the manuscript, its results, and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not talk about the manuscript with outsiders, use information prior to publication, or communicate with the authors directly. All comments should go only to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough reading and constructive tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the entire submission (including supplementary information) several times, take notes, then draft your response; keep criticism constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference specific parts of the manuscript (e.g., line numbers). Absolutely avoid being unnecessarily harsh or abusive; a peer-review is not the place to demonstrate wit or disrespect authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Introduction / Background: relevance, novelty, and citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the questions addressed meaningfully advance the field and whether the manuscript appropriately cites and frames prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for irrelevant studies, work that merely repeats well-known results, missing appropriate references, or inappropriate emphasis. Do your own literature search as if you were writing the paper; read cited studies you don't know and suggest missing citations. It's acceptable to recommend citing your own papers if appropriate, but don't demand self-serving citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Approach / Methods: completeness and replicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether methods and materials are described in enough detail for understanding and replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If details are missing, ask authors to provide them. Read outside sources on the methods if needed and, while respecting confidentiality, seek help understanding techniques. If you lack confidence in a methods assessment, tell the editor privately and request an additional expert reviewer for that portion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological soundness over perceived impact (journal-specific focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: For journals like PeerJ and PLOS ONE the emphasis is on scientific and methodological soundness rather than potential impact or readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge submissions primarily on correctness and rigor of methods and analysis, not on perceived importance. Align your comments with the journal's stated review criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting additional experiments: justification and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask for additional or modified experiments only if justified to verify reported results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider time, effort, and cost to authors; do not request experiments merely to slow a competing lab (this is unethical and can prompt formal complaints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting results and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether authors' interpretations are supported by the data and whether results are presented clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for more results or better presentation where needed. Recommend statistical or other domain-specific expert review if appropriate. Suggest moving material between Supplementary Information and main text when it improves clarity or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final checks: writing quality and compliance statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Check clarity, grammar, and associated statements (Funders, Ethics, Conflicts of Interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing is unclear or contains grammatical errors, request editing. Verify funder statements, ethics statements, conflict-of-interest disclosures, data availability statements (mechanism for making raw data available), and protections for human subjects; include these considerations in your report to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialist reviewers (statistical/technical expertise)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, recommend that the editor recruit a statistical or other technical expert to review parts of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe the data require a statistical expert (or another kind of expert), tell the editor and recommend such reviewers for a focused assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity vs open review: consider consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to sign your review; evaluate the pros and cons of open vs anonymous review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open review can increase effort, credit, and accountability; anonymity may make early-career researchers more comfortable critiquing colleagues. Signing reviews can provide public credit; the decision is personal and may be influenced by journal policies (PeerJ encourages but does not require open review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that peer review can continue after publication via community commenting platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication reviews (e.g., PubPeer, PubMed Commons) allow ongoing evaluation and replication; anyone can participate (subject to platform rules). This is a way to review work even if you were not invited pre-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional development: practice and learning from others
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve reviewing skills through practice, journal clubs, mentorship, and studying published review histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read peer-review histories posted by journals, browse comments on PeerJ/PubPeer/PubMed Commons, participate in journal clubs, and experience being an author to better understand the review process. Treat reviewing as a civic obligation to the scientific community.
